frictionVectors.title: European energy pressure
frictionVectors.details: Europe seeks reliable Algerian gas while pressing for greater supply flexibility and investment access. Algiers retains strong control over hydrocarbons but must balance export revenue against domestic consumption.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya strains Algeria's border security and diplomatic neutrality. External military involvement in the Sahel complicates Algiers' preference for regional autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic corridor rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting U.S., European, and Gulf interest as an alternative route for copper and cobalt exports from the DRC and Zambia. Angola gains leverage, but foreign financing and operators may limit long-term control.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and dependence on external operators constrain fiscal sovereignty. Diversification efforts are advancing, but debt exposure and infrastructure gaps remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou remains a critical trade gateway whose expansion depends heavily on foreign capital, contractors, and regional commerce. This creates leverage for external partners over customs, infrastructure, and supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel militant pressure
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups operating from the Sahel are increasing pressure along Benin's northern frontier and threatening transport corridors. Security partnerships are expanding, but reliance on outside intelligence and equipment is growing.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its negotiating position with major diamond partners, but public revenue remains exposed to global demand and producer concentration. The economy still needs diversification beyond diamonds.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-transition competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are pursuing Botswana's coal, copper, and battery-mineral potential. The government can set firm terms, though limited domestic processing capacity risks leaving value capture abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is asserting greater state control over gold production and challenging established foreign mining arrangements. This may increase public capture of rents but risks reduced investment, technical disruption, and opaque governance.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou is deepening security ties with Russia as relations with France and some Western partners deteriorate. The shift may preserve regime autonomy, but it brings uncertainty over mining access, accountability, and long-term infrastructure support.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state oversight and downstream value from nickel and rare-earth prospects, but limited capital and technical capacity leave room for external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Great Lakes security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Cross-border tensions involving eastern DRC armed groups continue to raise sovereignty risks and complicate transport, trade, and diplomatic maneuvering.

highlights: Atlantic logistics position is gaining value

frictionVectors.title: Strategic port and air access
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's ports, maritime domain, and air links attract competing interest from European, North American, and other external partners, creating pressure to balance security access with autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and water dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported fuel, desalination, and donor-backed infrastructure limits full sovereign control over essential systems despite relatively strong institutions.

highlights: Oil and gas remain state-controlled but externally financed
Transport corridors face persistent security stress

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and lenders remain central to offshore hydrocarbons, mining, and related infrastructure, while opaque contracting and limited local processing constrain domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Northern and Anglophone insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Far North and Northwest/Southwest disrupts roads, agricultural supply chains, and state access, increasing dependence on external security and humanitarian support.

highlights: Russian security partnership shapes strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and mining nexus
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has strengthened regime protection but is associated with opaque mineral arrangements and reduced transparency over sovereign resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-group control of corridors
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks continue to threaten roads, border zones, and artisanal mining areas, limiting state authority and raising dependence on foreign military support.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a security-centered state

frictionVectors.title: Oil dependence and concession leverage
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues and pipeline infrastructure remain vulnerable to external operators, price shocks, and financing conditions, limiting diversification and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external security ties
frictionVectors.details: Chad's position between Libya, Sudan, and the Sahel makes foreign military partnerships and logistics access central to national security, creating persistent sovereignty trade-offs.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration, maritime security, and development gaps keep the dispute active. France remains Comoros's most consequential external partner and a major source of aid and remittances.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL PORT AND FINANCE INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Comoros seeks investment in ports, energy, and transport from Gulf, Turkish, and other partners, but limited fiscal capacity reduces its bargaining power and increases dependence on external financing.

frictionVectors.title: M23–RWANDA SECURITY FRONT
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in eastern Congo continues to expose the state's limited control over territory and mineral corridors. Kinshasa's security partnerships and regional diplomacy remain constrained by accusations of external support for armed groups.

frictionVectors.title: COBALT AND COPPER CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater value capture and contract leverage in the copper-cobalt belt, but Chinese dominance, informal mining, and infrastructure bottlenecks continue to limit sovereign control over the strategic supply chain.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: State revenue and external bargaining power remain heavily tied to offshore oil, leaving the country exposed to price volatility and foreign technical and commercial operators. Diversification has not yet materially reduced this structural dependence.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese involvement in infrastructure and debt-linked projects around Pointe-Noire and national transport corridors provides needed capital but narrows fiscal and strategic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening domestic processing and producer regulation, but international buyers still capture much of the value from the cocoa chain. Climate stress and farm-level poverty add pressure to national resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port expansion and growing regional role attract Gulf, Chinese, European, and other investment. Competition for infrastructure and security partnerships is beneficial economically but creates pressure to balance external interests.

frictionVectors.title: BASES AND GREAT-POWER COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, gaining revenue and protection while facing reduced strategic autonomy and heightened exposure to regional crises.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEBT AND ETHIOPIAN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports remain essential to Ethiopia's trade, but transport and debt exposure—especially involving Chinese-financed infrastructure—creates vulnerability to shifts in Ethiopian demand and creditor leverage.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows, keeping water security tied to regional diplomacy and potential escalation.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, Gulf investment, and asset sales support fiscal stability but constrain policy autonomy over strategic infrastructure and state-owned assets.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling hydrocarbon output narrows fiscal space and increases pressure to attract foreign operators, often on terms that favor external capital and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and energy projects remain important, while debt exposure and limited transparency reduce sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline is increasingly affected by competition among Gulf, regional, and international actors, raising pressure over port access and security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other mineral projects provide revenue but rely heavily on foreign capital and operators, limiting domestic value capture despite strong political control.

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade routes, electricity links, labor mobility, and customs revenue remain closely tied to South Africa, constraining Eswatini's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and sugar exposure
frictionVectors.details: Manufacturing and sugar exports remain vulnerable to external market access rules, preference changes, and foreign-owned supply chains.

highlights: Debt and port access constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access dispute
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for dependable maritime access continues to generate tensions with Somalia and other regional actors, while inviting competing external security interests.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and investment pressure
frictionVectors.details: Debt negotiations and foreign-exchange shortages increase reliance on international lenders, while liberalization and telecom investment create trade-offs between capital inflows and strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: French Influence Reset
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is renegotiating the political and commercial balance with France while seeking more diversified partnerships. Security and mining ties remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-to-Industry Gap
frictionVectors.details: Gabon retains stronger control over oil, manganese, and timber policy, but limited domestic processing and transport capacity still leave value capture dependent on foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Strategic Asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade routes, security coordination, and regional access. This improves stability but constrains independent infrastructure and foreign-policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Coastal Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Banjul’s capacity and river access remain bottlenecks for trade, while external financing is central to port and road upgrades. Debt, concession terms, and customs control are persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Water Security
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage rivers, farmland, and public legitimacy while exposing gaps in enforcement. The government faces pressure to confront politically connected actors and foreign-linked mining networks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Accra is seeking greater domestic value capture from gold, lithium, and other minerals through refining and local-content rules. Fiscal stress, Chinese commercial influence, and investor demands complicate implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore corridor is bringing rail, port, and mining investment at unprecedented scale, but Chinese and multinational capital will shape logistics and revenue flows for decades. Contract transparency and local processing remain major sovereignty tests.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Enclave Economy
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains heavily dependent on foreign firms for bauxite extraction and export infrastructure. The junta’s tougher stance may raise state receipts but has not yet resolved environmental damage or domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Narcotics and Port Capture
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime enforcement leave the country exposed to transnational cocaine trafficking and elite capture of port and customs channels. This directly erodes fiscal sovereignty and security autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains reliant on raw cashew exports and external buyers, leaving producers vulnerable to price shocks and opaque brokerage networks. Limited processing capacity prevents meaningful domestic control of resource rents.

highlights: Ports and minerals drive strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is seeking to preserve control over Mombasa and other strategic infrastructure while renegotiating the fiscal burden of externally financed projects. Beijing remains an important lender and contractor, but Nairobi is diversifying toward Gulf, Western and multilateral financing.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in Kenya's titanium, niobium, graphite and rare-earth prospects is increasing. The government faces pressure to secure greater domestic processing and revenue while avoiding regulatory uncertainty that could deter investment.

highlights: Water sovereignty tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports and dam construction provide essential revenue but deepen Lesotho's structural dependence on South Africa. Delays, cost overruns and disputes over pricing and royalties can constrain sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Manufacturing and trade-preference exposure
frictionVectors.details: The textile sector depends heavily on foreign-owned firms and preferential access to external markets, especially the United States. Any shift in trade preferences or regional logistics costs could rapidly weaken employment and fiscal stability.

highlights: Ports and concessions attract Gulf interest

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore operations and proposed expansions are central to Liberia's growth strategy, but foreign operators retain substantial control over capital, logistics and export chains. The government is under pressure to improve local processing, revenue collection and community benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia and Buchanan are becoming more important to external investors seeking Atlantic access and regional supply routes. Liberia must balance concession financing against risks of opaque contracts, limited domestic participation and strategic dependence.

highlights: Oil remains hostage to political fragmentation

frictionVectors.title: Oil blockade and institutional division
frictionVectors.details: Competing authorities and armed groups continue to treat production, export terminals and budget flows as leverage. The National Oil Corporation remains a key unifying institution, but interruptions and contested appointments threaten sovereign control over the main revenue source.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates and European actors retain significant influence through security partnerships, bases, diplomacy and energy interests. External backing reduces incentives for a unified national security architecture and complicates infrastructure planning.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, cobalt and ilmenite dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining projects provide export earnings but leave Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles, imported inputs and disputes over taxes, water use and local benefits. The state is seeking stronger downstream participation without undermining already fragile investment flows.

frictionVectors.title: Power infrastructure and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and the weakness of the national utility limit industrial and public-sector autonomy. Madagascar relies on external lenders, donors and private operators to stabilize generation and grids, increasing vulnerability to financing and contract disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and donor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditionality constrain fiscal sovereignty, while Malawi remains heavily dependent on external budget and balance-of-payments support.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are positioning around uranium, rare earths and graphite, but weak infrastructure and regulatory capacity limit Malawi's ability to capture value locally.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The ruling junta relies on Russian security assistance and African Corps-linked support, increasing Moscow's influence over security policy and strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: Mining contract confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Disputes with foreign mining companies, especially over gold taxation and operating rights, are boosting state control but risking investment, production and export revenues.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas project dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and BP-led partners offers major revenue potential, but offshore delays, partner dependence and limited domestic processing constrain sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and migration leverage
frictionVectors.details: European support for migration control and the planned regional electricity and transport corridors give Mauritania bargaining power while also increasing external influence over infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos implementation risk
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty arrangement over the Chagos Archipelago strengthens Mauritius's territorial claim, but the Diego Garcia base, lease terms and implementation remain sensitive to UK and US interests.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius must balance expanding Indian, Chinese, British and US interest in maritime surveillance, ports and ocean resources without surrendering control of its exclusive economic zone.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and investment in the territory drive diplomatic gains and resource development, but remain contested by Algeria and the Polisario Front and complicate relations with Europe.

frictionVectors.title: External industrial dependence
frictionVectors.details: Automotive, renewable-energy and desalination expansion strengthens Morocco's industrial base, while European supply chains, foreign technology and water stress limit full strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Enclave Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas project remains strategically important but is dominated by foreign operators, financing, and security requirements. Any restart could boost state revenues while deepening perceptions that local communities bear the risks without proportional benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency and External Security
frictionVectors.details: Islamist militancy in Cabo Delgado continues to threaten energy infrastructure and civilian authority. Foreign military and private-security involvement improves protection but exposes limits in Mozambique's sovereign security capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy Capital
frictionVectors.details: Recent oil discoveries and green-hydrogen plans could transform public finances, but projects rely heavily on international majors, lenders, and export partners. Namibia is seeking stronger local-content and revenue terms before committing to large-scale development.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Walvis Bay is becoming more valuable for regional logistics and critical-mineral exports, drawing competition among Western, Chinese, and regional interests. Infrastructure expansion creates leverage for Namibia but also pressure over strategic access and ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is renegotiating foreign mining relationships and asserting greater control over uranium and other strategic resources. This may improve bargaining power, but sanctions, technical constraints, and investor exits threaten near-term production.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger's break with France and closer security ties with Russia and Sahel partners have reduced Western influence while increasing dependence on alternative external patrons. Persistent jihadist violence limits the state's ability to secure territory, infrastructure, and trade corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil Capital and Output Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Regulatory reform and new investment are intended to restore production, but foreign operators, crude theft, pipeline sabotage, and opaque contracting continue to weaken effective state control. The government remains exposed to global price swings and external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and Infrastructure Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining expansion, especially around large private capacity, could reduce dependence on imported fuel and strengthen industrial sovereignty. Power shortages, port congestion, pipeline insecurity, and disputes over market access remain major constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo generate sustained diplomatic pressure and sanctions risk. Kigali presents its policy as a security imperative, while critics argue that regional instability facilitates externalized resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Aid, Investment, and Sovereignty Trade-off
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control over development and attracts substantial foreign investment, but its model remains reliant on aid, concessional finance, and international partnerships. Governance criticism and conditionality can constrain Kigali's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Exploration partnerships with foreign energy firms offer potential revenue but leave São Tomé and Príncipe dependent on external capital, technology, and licensing terms. Commercial discoveries remain uncertain.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago's location attracts interest from Portugal, China, and Gulf of Guinea security partners. Limited naval and fiscal capacity constrains its ability to independently police offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas production is strengthening Dakar's bargaining position, while the government seeks greater local participation and contract transparency. Renegotiation risks tension with international operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure commitments and fiscal stress limit policy autonomy despite growing hydrocarbon revenues. Financing from multilateral institutions, China, Europe, and Gulf partners remains strategically important.

frictionVectors.title: External Maritime Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on India, France, the United States, and other partners for maritime surveillance and anti-piracy support. This improves control over its vast maritime zone but creates dependence on outside security infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, telecommunications, and tourism investments attract competing Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf interests. Victoria is attempting to preserve strategic autonomy while avoiding excessive financial exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Revenue Capture
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain central to export earnings, but foreign capital and commodity-price volatility limit domestic value capture. The government faces pressure to improve taxation, local processing, and contract oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Freetown Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port modernization and mining-export corridors involve substantial external financing and operators, particularly from Chinese and other international firms. Infrastructure expansion improves connectivity while increasing exposure to creditor and concession leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Licensing Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is promoting offshore petroleum exploration, but federal-state disagreements, security risks, and limited regulatory capacity complicate control over licensing and future revenues. Foreign operators remain essential for capital, technology, and risk absorption.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Architecture
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, the African Union, and other partners provide military, port, and maritime support. These relationships strengthen state capacity but can pull Mogadishu into competing regional agendas and constrain independent resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL PROCESSING AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation of platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth inputs while balancing investment from China, the United States, and European partners.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Weak freight rail and port performance continues to reduce sovereign control over mineral export chains and increases reliance on private operators and external logistics partners.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to Sudan war

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on infrastructure crossing Sudan to export crude, leaving production and state revenue vulnerable to conflict, sabotage, and bargaining by external operators.

frictionVectors.title: OIL-REVENUE AND SECURITY NETWORKS
frictionVectors.details: Political elites, armed groups, and foreign commercial interests compete over oil revenues and transport corridors, limiting transparent national control of resources.

highlights: Gold and ports attract competing patrons

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival armed networks, while external buyers and regional intermediaries capture value outside accountable state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and related infrastructure has strategic value for Gulf, regional, and other foreign actors, increasing pressure on whichever authority controls the coastline.

highlights: Ports and gas corridors gain strategic weight

frictionVectors.title: LNG AND INFRASTRUCTURE NEGOTIATIONS
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is attempting to secure larger domestic benefits from natural-gas development while managing foreign investor demands, fiscal terms, and environmental concerns.

frictionVectors.title: PORT CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Upgrades around Dar es Salaam and proposed regional corridors could strengthen national leverage, but financing and construction partnerships may create long-term exposure to external creditors and operators.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRANSIT INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé gives Togo strategic relevance in West African trade, but dependence on foreign shipping, finance, and logistics firms limits full sovereign control over the corridor.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate resources remain central to export earnings, while questions over processing capacity, contract transparency, and external commercial participation constrain domestic value capture.

highlights: Phosphate and fiscal sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains closely tied to Tunisia’s management of migration routes. This creates recurring sovereignty concerns over border enforcement and domestic policy priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: High financing needs and dependence on imported energy constrain policy autonomy. Delays in external financing and weak investment in domestic production increase exposure to outside creditors and suppliers.

highlights: Oil development advances despite external pressure

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline remains central to Uganda’s resource strategy but faces legal, activist, and financing pressure from Western institutions. Uganda is responding by relying more heavily on regional and non-Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand Uganda’s infrastructure base while increasing repayment and strategic-dependence risks. Domestic value capture remains limited outside construction and services.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors for copper and cobalt assets is giving Lusaka more negotiating leverage. However, most value is still captured through foreign capital, technology, and processing networks.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and support from international lenders improve short-term stability but constrain spending and industrial-policy choices. Rising mineral revenues have not yet fully translated into broad sovereign control of the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Concession Competition
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using licensing and export restrictions to demand greater domestic processing of lithium, platinum, and other minerals. Limited capital, sanctions-related constraints, and opaque concession practices reduce the state’s ability to capture consistent value.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and External Finance Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability and restricted access to conventional finance encourage reliance on commodity-backed deals and politically connected investors. This weakens transparency and leaves strategic infrastructure vulnerable to external bargaining.
